paper_title: MetaRubric: Learning to Reward for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Rubric-based reinforcement learning extends reward-driven optimization to open-ended tasks by assigning partial credit to individual response requirements. However, rubric judges can assign a high criterion score even when the information or action it requires is absent from the response, a failure mode we term Vacuous Credit. Such awards persist after the required information is removed and can reverse the sign of a response's GRPO advantage. To address this problem, we introduce MetaRubric, which alternates evidence-aware policy optimization with response-guided rubric adaptation. We construct counterfactual counterparts by changing one task-relevant fact in each prompt. During policy optimization, credit is assigned only when the response contains sufficient evidence to satisfy the required rubric criterion. After each policy-optimization stage, current policy responses guide revisions to original and counterfactual criteria while preserving the meaning of the original prompt's initial rubric as interpreted under each prompt's facts. We also adapt criterion weights at stage boundaries to better address observed policy errors. Across multiple backbones, MetaRubric improves PubMedQA accuracy by 6.00--20.40 percentage points over static-judge GRPO, with further gains on HealthBench-Hard and two multimodal medical benchmarks.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Rubric-based reinforcement learning extends reward-driven optimization to openended tasks by assigning partial credit to individual response requirements. However, rubric judges can assign high criterion score even when the information or action it requires is absent from the response, failure mode we term Vacuous Credit. Such awards persist after the required information is removed and can reverse the sign of responses GRPO advantage. To address this problem, we introduce MetaRubric, which alternates evidence-aware policy optimization with response-guided rubric adaptation. We construct counterfactual counterparts by changing one task-relevant fact in each prompt. During policy optimization, credit is assigned only when the response contains sufficient evidence to satisfy the required rubric criterion. After each policy-optimization stage, current policy responses guide revisions to original and counterfactual criteria while preserving the meaning of the original prompts initial rubric as interpreted under each prompts facts. We also adapt criterion weights at stage boundaries to better address observed policy errors. Across multiple backbones, MetaRubric improves PubMedQA accuracy by 6.0020.40 percentage points over static-judge GRPO, with further gains on HealthBench-Hard and two multimodal medical benchmarks.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) provides fine-grained rewards for open-ended tasks by assigning partial credit across instance-specific response criteria (Liu et al., 2026; Shan & Shao, 2026). language-model judge evaluates these criteria, and their weighted scores provide the reward used to optimize the policy, even for tasks with multiple valid responses and no single automatically verifiable answer (Gunjal et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2025). critical challenge arises when the reward credits information or actions absent from the response, so that policy optimization favors responses that fail important requirements (Mahmoud et al., 2026). Fig. 1(a) illustrates failure mode observed in our rubric-judge evaluations. Consider patient asking how often to attend checkups after stent procedure and whether the schedule varies by region. The rubric requires the model to ask for the patients location, yet the model only notes that guidelines differ across regions and provides no checkup frequency. The judge nevertheless marks the location criterion as satisfied, awarding credit for an action the model never performed. This poses two problems in rubric-based judging. (1) Criterion underspecification: the rubric may not clearly define the task-specific requirements or the observable evidence needed for credit. As result, awards can persist even after all information required by criterion is removed from the response (Sec. 3.2). (2) Unsupported judging: the judge may award credit for information or actions absent from the response, distorting the relative rewards used for policy optimization (Sec. 3.3). We call this broader failure Vacuous Credit: judge assigns high criterion score even though the response omits information or an action required to satisfy it. Such erroneous credit corrupts the learning signal: within group relative policy optimization (GRPO) rollout group, correcting Corresponding author. 1 Preprint. Figure 1: Motivation and overview of MetaRubric. (a) Vacuous Credit in rubric-based RL. Under an incomplete, underspecified criterion, the judge awards full credit to safe, conservative response that leaves the query unanswered. (b) MetaRubric addresses this by jointly improving the policy and rubric: the inner loop optimizes evidence-aware responses, while the outer loop reweights criterion groups and revises criterion descriptions.This produces clearer criteria and more concrete answers. single erroneous award can flip the sign of responses advantage, reversing its contribution to the policy update. Repeated optimization can therefore favor responses that score well under the grading procedure without satisfying the intended requirement. To address this challenge, we introduce MetaRubric, which alternates an inner loop of evidenceaware policy optimization with an outer loop of rubric adaptation (Fig. 1(b)). Each prompt is paired with counterfactual that changes one task-relevant fact, exposing which requirements depend on that fact. In the inner loop, the policy is optimized under the current rubric. For each criterion, the judge assigns three scores: satisfaction, requirement coverage, and evidential support. Credit is bounded by the minimum of these three scores. The resulting rubric reward is combined with an auxiliary question-answering (QA) score to optimize the policy with GRPO. At the end of each training stage, the outer loop updates the rubric in two steps. First, error-guided weight adaptation adjusts criterion-group weights based on observed policy errors, subject to magnitude bounds and severity-order constraints. Second, semantically anchored rubric revision updates criterion descriptions or correspondence labels using collected responses, while preserving the requirements of the initial rubric for each prompt. Only revisions that improve agreement with held-out reference judgments and pass semantic review are accepted. The resulting weights and revisions define the rubric configurations for the next training stage. We evaluate MetaRubric on text-only and multimodal medical benchmarks across multiple LLM and MLLM backbones. Across baselines, MetaRubric improves PubMedQA accuracy by 6.00 20.40 points, HealthBench-Hard accuracy by 2.463.19 points, MMOral-X by 1.292.13 points, and MMOral-OPG by 3.093.82 points.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Rubric-based Reinforcement Learning. Rubrics as Rewards (Gunjal et al., 2026) extends onpolicy RL to open-ended tasks using instance-specific criteria. RubricHub and OpenRubrics scale criterion generation (Li et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Yuxuan et al., 2026), while RRD refines their granularity and weights (Shen et al., 2026). Reward generation also uses pairwise adaptive criteria (Jia et al., 2026), policy self-grading (Ye et al., 2025), and joint optimization of rubric generators with reasoners (Sheng et al., 2026; Guan et al., 2026) or judges (Xu et al., 2026). On the other hand, MetaRubric couples evidence-aware policy optimization with response-guided rubric adaptation. 2 Preprint. Figure 2: Reward growth and rubric satisfaction. (a,b) Training reward and rubric scores during training; evaluation uses panel of three stronger judges on separate test set. Panels (a,c) use GPT4o-mini as the training judge; panels (b,d) use GPT-5.4-mini. (c,d) Changes from step 0 in fully satisfied requirement weight and Vacuous Credit identified using stronger model to audit response evidence. Both are normalized by total available rubric credit Px and expressed in percentage points. Policy errors drive criterion revision on original and counterfactual cases, as well as criterion-group reweighting, while preserving the initial rubrics intended requirements. Reward Hacking in Rubric-based RL. Proxy reward gains can diverge from response quality (Gao et al., 2023). Chasing the Tail (Zhang et al., 2026) improves rubric discrimination among highquality responses, while Mahmoud et al. (2026) distinguish verifier failures from rubric-design limitations. Mitigations include deterministic verification with restricted input exposure in RLR3 (Yu et al., 2026b) and random criterion dropout during RL (Yang et al., 2026a). We identify Vacuous Credit, in which judge assigns high criterion score to empty assurances, generic safety advice, or defensive qualifications even when the required content is entirely absent. Content-deletion tests and recorded-group replay connect this judgment error to policy optimization: an award can survive removal of its evidence, and removing an absent-content award can reverse GRPO advantage sign (Sec. 3). MetaRubric makes content coverage and support explicit components of credit assignment and uses policy responses to adapt the rubric during training.

We independently measure rubric satisfaction using stronger judges to audit the test responses, defined as the normalized weight of fully satisfied criteria. Fig. 2(c,d) shows that rubric satisfaction fluctuates but declines overall as training reward increases, whereas auditor-flagged Vacuous Credit persists throughout training. These trajectories reveal that omitted content can still receive credit during training. We next examine this failure through controlled evidence removal. 3.2 VACUOUS CREDIT PERSISTS AFTER REQUIRED EVIDENCE IS REMOVED Finding 2: Most criterion awards persist after the required content is removed. To directly verify whether criterion credit depends on the required evidence, we perform deletion test. Given 1,000 policy rollouts judged correct during training, we use GPT-5.5 to generate two paired edits of each response. Required-content deletion removes all information or actions needed to satisfy the target criterion while retaining generic statements , whereas the control, Genericstatement deletion removes statements that do not fulfill the target requirement while preserving the required content. We score the intact and edited responses using the reward judges and training reward prompt from Sec. 3.1. For each judge, award retention is the percentage of target criteria credited in the intact response that remain credited after deletion. As shown in Tab. 1, GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5.4-mini retain 82.0% and 69.8% of target-criterion awards after requiredcontent deletion. Thus, removing required content lowers retention compared with the controlled setting, yet most awards persist even when the target requirement is no longer satisfied. These retained awards constitute Vacuous Credit and directly affect the learning signal used for policy optimization. 3.3 IMPLICATIONS FOR POLICY OPTIMIZATION Table 1: Retention rate of targetcriterion awards in the deletion test. GRPO computes each responses advantage relative to the other responses in its rollout group, so this error can change which responses are reinforced. response that omits required action but receives Vacuous Credit can match or exceed the reward of response that performs it, and then receives an equal or larger advantage despite its lower rubric satisfaction. When such awards recur across rollout groups, policy updates can reinforce generic statements in place of the specific information or actions the rubric requires. Criterion credit should therefore depend on requirement coverage and evidential support before rewards are compared within group. 4 Preprint. Figure 3: Overview of MetaRubric. sections.title: 4 METARUBRIC: LEARNING TO REWARD FOR RUBRIC-BASED RL
sections.content: MetaRubric addresses Vacuous Credit discussed in Sec. 3 with two ideas: criterion earns credit only for content the response actually provides and can support, and the rubric itself adapts to the errors the policy keeps making. MetaRubric alternates between evidence-aware policy optimization in an inner loop and rubric adaptation in an outer loop  (Fig. 3)  . The inner loop trains the policy with GRPO, using reward that caps criterion credit by requirement coverage and evidential support (Sec. 4.1). Training prompts come in pairs: each original prompt is paired with counterfactual that changes one task-relevant fact, thus responses must attend to the facts on which requirements depend. At the end of each stage, error-guided weight adaptation shifts weight toward criterion groups the policy fails more often (Sec. 4.2). Semantically anchored rubric revision then clarifies ambiguous criterion descriptions without changing their core semantics (Sec. 4.3). Stage-wise alternation. Training of MetaRubric proceeds in stages = 0, 1, . . .. Within stage t, the rubric configuration Φt = (Et, τt) is fixed. Here, Et contains each criterion description and its correspondence label (Sec. 4.1), while τt contains one log-weight adjustment per criterion group (Sec. 4.2). Let θt denote the policy parameters at the start of stage t. Each stage performs θt+1 = UGRPO(θt; Φt), Φt+1 = A(Φt; Bt, Vt), (3) where UGRPO denotes GRPO updates under Φt, Bt is the set of policy responses collected during these updates, and Vt is set of held-out validation cases. The adaptation step first updates τt from the errors in Bt and then accepts proposed criterion revision when it passes validation on Vt. 4.1 EVIDENCE-AWARE POLICY OPTIMIZATION The inner loop ties the training reward to prompt-specific content that the response actually contains and can support, rather than to generic content that merely appears to meet criterion (Inner loop in Fig. 3). Counterfactual prompt pairs expose which requirements depend on specific prompt facts. The evidence-aware rubric reward credits criterion only when its coverage and support checks pass, while an auxiliary QA reward independently checks whether the relevant facts appear in the response. GRPO then optimizes the policy using the combined reward. Counterfactual prompt pairs. To ground credit in prompt-specific facts, we pair each prompt with counterfactual xcf that changes one task-relevant fact while holding the remaining context constant (e.g., the stated age changes from 40 to 60 in Fig. 3). sections.title: 4.3 SEMANTICALLY ANCHORED RUBRIC REVISION
sections.content: Reweighting cannot fix loosely worded criterion: if it reads considers the patients location rather than asks for the patients location, response that merely notes regional differences keeps earning Vacuous Credit at any weight. Policy responses expose such wording, but revising the rubric from them risks drifting toward what the policy already does. We therefore let revisions clarify wording but not requirements, and accept them only after held-out validation (Revise rubric). Propose one revision. The original prompts initial rubric serves as the semantic anchor, and the correspondence labels specify how each anchored requirement reads under the counterfactuals facts. Given the anchor, current rubric, prompt, and response from Bt, the proposer rewrites one ambiguous or mismatched criterion description. It also updates the correspondence label when necessary. Validate and accept. revision is accepted only if it improves agreement with reference panel by more than δ on the held-out responses in Vt. separate semantic review must also confirm that the revision preserves the anchored requirement and remains consistent with the prompts facts. Otherwise the current description is retained; the updated weights carry over either way.

sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 5.1 SETUP Benchmarks. We evaluate text-only medical QA on PubMedQA (Jin et al., 2019) and HealthBenchHard (Arora et al., 2025), and multimodal diagnosis and visual QA on MMOral-X (Fan et al., 2026) and MMOral-OPG (Hao et al., 2026), respectively. Dataset splits, rubric construction, and evaluation details appear in Secs. A.2.1 and A.2.5. Metrics. We report PubMedQA accuracy, HealthBench-Hard accuracy-axis score, MMOral-X mean score across three difficulty subsets, and MMOral-OPG overall score (one evaluation). GPT5.5 serves as the strong judge for all model-based test-set evaluations. Auxiliary QA accuracy (Aux. Acc.) measures the Qwen3-1.7B readers pooled accuracy on accepted multiple-choice questions given the model response; invalid outputs count as incorrect. Baselines. We compare MetaRubric with four policies: GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) with static judge, DAPO (Yu et al., 2026a), Dr. GRPO (Liu et al., 2025), and GSPO (Zheng et al., 2025). We use Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025) for text-only tasks, their Qwen3-VL counterparts (Bai et al., 2025) for multimodal tasks, and Gemma-e2b (Gemma Team et al., 2026) for both. 5.2 MAIN RESULTS MetaRubric improves over static-judge GRPO in all 21 model-familymetric comparisons in Tab. 2, spanning categorical answers, rubric-graded conversations, and visual question answering. These results support both adapting how requirements are expressed and prioritized and checking whether the content credited by the rubric is supported. 5.4 DEEP ANALYSIS Rubric revision analysis. Tab. 3 summarizes criterion revisions during training on HealthBench, PubMedQA and MMOral-RL. Each criterion is counted once if its description or correspondence label changes at least once; repeated edits do not increase the count, and weight-only updates are excluded. Average lengths are measured in whitespace-separated words across all criterion descriptions before and after training. Revision affects 45.2% of HealthBench criteria, 29.8% of PubMedQA criteria and 60.6% of MMOral-RL criteria. Its reach varies substantially across tasks: majority of criteria change on MMOral-RL, compared with fewer than one third on PubMedQA. Average descriptions grow by 5.5, 3.9 and 5.6 words, respectively, corresponding to increases of 13.5%, 27.3% and 33.1%. The fraction of criteria left unchanged ranges from 39.4% on MMOralRL to 70.2% on PubMedQA, showing that revision selectively modifies the rubric rather than rewriting every criterion. Revision rate does not simply decrease with initial description length: MMOralRL starts with longer descriptions than PubMedQA but revises larger fraction of criteria. These statistics establish the extent of adaptation; the case study below illustrates how revision makes the required evidence and the scope of claim explicit. 9 Preprint. Is the Final Rubric Sufficient? We test whether MetaRubrics gains can be recovered by retraining with its final rubric alone, without further adaptation. As shown in Tab. 4, the final rubric improves HealthBench-Hard accuracy from 8.83 to 9.04 and MMOral-OPG overall score from 20.59 to 21.78, whereas MetaRubric reaches 13.02 and 26.35, respectively. Relative to the baseline, final-rubric retraining recovers 5.0% and 20.7% of MetaRubrics gains, computed as the final-rubric gain divided by the full-method gain. The learned rubric alone is therefore insufficient to reproduce the full methods performance in these runs. This is consistent with benefit from matching the rubric to the policys evolving errors: requirements emphasized late in training may provide different learning signal when applied from the outset. These results suggest that the sequence of rubric updates is itself part of the valuable and effective learning procedure. Case Study. Fig. 5 shows how an evidence criterion specifies the reported absence of motion differences, while an overstatement penalty names unsupported leftright and superoinferior claims. For an illustrative stage with more overstatement than evidence-use errors, relative group weighting shifts the evidence criterion from +6 to +5 and the penalty from 6 to 8. The revision identifies which claims the evidence supports, while reweighting changes how strongly the remaining errors influence optimization. Increasing the penalty alone would leave its interpretation unchanged; clarifying its wording alone would leave its relative priority unchanged. The example thus illustrates why criterion descriptions and weights provide distinct controls over the reward.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We identify Vacuous Credit as failure mode in rubric-based reinforcement learning, where judges assign high criterion scores even when the information or action required by criterion is absent from the response. Our analyses show that criterion credit can persist after the required information is removed, and that correcting an erroneous award can reverse responses GRPO advantage. To address this mismatch between rubric credit and response evidence, we introduce MetaRubric, which combines evidence-aware scoring with response-guided criterion revision and criterion-group weights that adapt to observed policy errors. Across text-only and multimodal medical tasks, MetaRubric consistently improves over static-rubric GRPO baselines, supporting the use of explicit checks for required information and actions alongside rubric adaptation.

sections.content: Contents A.1: Limitations A.2: Implementation and Experimental Details A.3: Prompt Templates A.4: Auxiliary Question Examples A.1 LIMITATIONS Single seed. Each training configuration uses one seed; the reported results do not quantify variation across training runs. Comparison scope. Many related works have not released their training code, preventing direct comparisons under matched experimental settings. A. IMPLEMENTATION AND EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS A.2.1 DEPLOYMENT DETAILS PubMedQA. We train on the non-test portion of PubMedQAs expert-labeled PQA-L subset (Jin et al., 2019), reserving label-stratified validation split and retaining the official test set for evaluation. Each input contains the question and its abstract context. For each original training example, we construct rubric from six-criterion template, inserting its reference label into the decision criterion. The three positive criteria reward the correct decision, accurate use of abstract evidence, and relevance to the question and study details. The three negative criteria penalize unsupported claims, contradictions or overstatements of the abstract, and missing or generic rationale. The supplied abstract is the evidence source for assessing the rationale. HealthBench. We use HealthBench (Arora et al., 2025) conversations outside HealthBench-Hard for training and validation, keeping the Hard subset for evaluation. Each conversations initial rubric uses the official physician-written criteria and signed point values. MMOral-RL. For both MMOral-X and MMOral-OPG, we train on the reinforcement-learning training set from OralGPT-Plus (Fan et al., 2026), which we denote as MMOral-RL. The two benchmarks evaluate models trained on this shared training set. MMOral-RL contains 980 original training examples with 8,672 rubric criteria. Each example has 8.85 criteria on average, with median of 8 and range of 139. We generate the initial MMOral-RL rubrics using procedure informed by the coarse-to-fine rubric construction approach of RubricHub (Li et al., 2026). These task-specific rubrics provide the starting criteria for reward computation and subsequent rubric adaptation. A.2.2 AUXILIARY QUESTION CONSTRUCTION The auxiliary QA tasks in Sec. 4.1 assess whether response provides the information needed to answer questions about its source case. We use auxiliary QA for HealthBench-Hard, MMOral-X, and MMOral-OPG. PubMedQA already provides definite reference label (yes/no/maybe) for each question, so we evaluate its answers directly and do not construct auxiliary questions or report Aux. Acc. for it. We construct these questions from benchmark reference answers and annotations, using Qwen3-1.7B as the reader. Question-only screening measures whether this reader can answer without the response; the evaluation-bank acceptance rules are specified below. Training and evaluation questions use their respective source entries for target extraction, generation, and content review; the MMOral evaluation extension is kept separate from the training bank. The auxiliary questions and their scoring rules are fixed before training and do not change during rubric adaptation. Section A.4 shows example questions from the three evaluation banks. Source-grounded target extraction. For each benchmark entry, we decompose the reference answer or annotations into independently testable facts. Each auxiliary question targets distinct fact or coherent group of facts, and questions associated with the same entry cover complementary information rather than paraphrasing one another. The number of questions therefore depends on the 13 Preprint. available non-overlapping targets, rather than requiring the same number for every entry. We retain source identifier, target identifier, and the supporting source facts for each question throughout construction. For the MMOral extension, the benchmark entry provides the reference for content verification. Multiple-choice generation and content review. generator converts each target into fouroption question with one correct answer and three distractors. It receives the source material, reference answer, target facts, other targets from the same entry, and any revision feedback, but no response from model being evaluated. separate content-review call checks that the question preserves its target, that the source supports the correct option, and that this option fully answers the question. The review also requires mutually exclusive options with exactly one correct answer, plausible distractors of comparable form, and no answer cues from option length or wording. Questions must remain complementary to the other questions for the entry. Unsupported facts, ambiguous questions, and changes to the meaning of the correct answer are rejected. Screening without the response. After content review, Qwen3-1.7B receives only the question and its options, labeled AD. The response, reference answer, and correct option label are withheld. We use the same reader checkpoint, prompt, decoding configuration, and option order throughout screening. question passes only if the reader returns valid single option letter that differs from the reference answer. correct prediction or an invalid output fails the screen. For the evaluation banks in Tab. 5, HealthBench-Hard uses content-reviewed questions without requiring questiononly screening pass. Each MMOral bank retains all constructed questions once its valid-wrong rate exceeds 90%, including questions the reader answers correctly. Target-preserving revision. For question that fails screening, the generator may jointly revise the question and all three distractors. The source and target identifiers, tested facts, correct answer content, and correct option position remain unchanged. Each revised candidate undergoes content review before the same reader test is repeated. Revisions may remove unintended cues or improve the alternatives, but cannot introduce ambiguity or unsupported content. Once version passes both checks, we accept it and make no further revisions based on subsequent evaluation scores. Response-conditioned evaluation. For each accepted question, the same reader receives previously generated response from the model being evaluated, together with the final question and options, and returns one option letter; it is instructed to answer using only the response, without filling in missing information from outside knowledge. We compute auxiliary QA accuracy (Aux. Acc.) by dividing the total number of correct predictions by the total number of accepted tasks evaluated, counting invalid outputs as incorrect. Accuracy is pooled over tasks, without first averaging within source entries or revision rounds, and correctness is determined by exact option matching without an LLM judge. This evaluation accuracy is distinct from the point-weighted training score RQA in Eq. (6). It measures response-supported question answering with the specified reader and is reported alongside the original benchmark metrics. Benchmark and split statistics. Table 5 reports the constructed questions in the three evaluation banks. HealthBench-Hard has 4,117 questions covering 965 of its 1,000 source entries; the remaining 35 entries have no extracted targets. MMOral-X and MMOral-OPG have 828 and 981 questions, respectively, covering all source entries. Mean questions per entry uses the full source split, including entries with no questions. Each response is scored with its own prompts rubric. For response with reward Rj from Eq. The advantage measures how far responses reward lies above or below the group mean, scaled by the within-group reward variation. The resulting advantages enter the clipped GRPO objective to update the policy. Hyperparameters. At each boundary, the outer loop estimates group errors from at most 96 responses, using one response per sampled prompt, and updates weights with η = 0.1. proposed revision requires 20 distinct validation cases and case-balanced agreement gain strictly greater than δ = 0.02, as well as semantic approval. The proposer receives neither the held-out responses nor their reference judgments. The inner judge and outer grading, proposal, semantic-review, and referencepanel roles use GPT-5.4-mini; outer roles use separate calls with temperature zero. Execution and checkpointing. The configuration uses two GPUs for policy training with FSDP2 and tensor-parallel rollout generation, with actor parameters and optimizer states offloaded to CPU. Gradient checkpointing and FlashAttention are enabled. Checkpoints save the model, optimizer, and training state, allowing the next segment to resume after rubric update. The software stack is verl 0.8.0.dev, PyTorch 2.8.0 (CUDA 12.8), vLLM 0.11.0, Transformers 4.57.6, and FlashAttention 2.8.3. A.2.5 EVALUATION PROTOCOLS AND METRICS Test-set judge. GPT-5.5 serves as the strong judge for all model-based test-set evaluations in Sec. 5. Text-only benchmarks. PubMedQA (Jin et al., 2019) provides biomedical questions with yes/no/maybe answers. We evaluate accuracy on its 500-question expert-labeled test set, providing the abstract context with each question. A.3 PROMPT TEMPLATES The following templates cover rubric and counterfactual construction, auxiliary QA, evidence-aware scoring, and rubric adaptation. Braced fields denote task-specific inputs; image inputs accompany the corresponding multimodal query. A.3.1 DATA AND AUXILIARY QUESTION CONSTRUCTION Initial Rubric Construction System prompt Construct task-specific rubric from the supplied prompt, reference answer, and annotations. Use the source as the factual authority. If source rubric is supplied, preserve its requirements, scoring polarity, and priorities. Each criterion must specify an observable response requirement or an undesirable behavior. Cover distinct requirements without duplicating credit. Preserve conditions, quantities, negations, and uncertainty. Do not introduce unsupported facts or clinical inferences. Assign stable criterion_id and severity: nice_to_have, should_have, must_have, or contraindication. State whether the criterion describes desired content or an undesirable behavior, and identify its supporting source facts. Return JSON with rubrics, each containing criterion_id, criterion, severity, polarity, and source_support. Do not use candidate responses to define requirements. Query prompt Prompt and supplied evidence: {prompt} Reference answer and annotations: {reference} Source rubric, if available: {source_rubric} Figure 6: Initial Rubric Construction prompt. Counterfactual Prompt and Rubric Construction System prompt Create one counterfactual by changing exactly one task-relevant fact. Hold the remaining context fixed. Update the reference answer and fact-dependent rubric criteria only as required by that intervention. Preserve unchanged criteria verbatim and retain the original rubric as the semantic anchor. Record the changed fact before and after the intervention. For each criterion, specify whether it is invariant, changes target, changes weight, becomes inapplicable, or becomes applicable. Preserve its correspondence to the original requirement. Do not invent additional findings, change unrelated requirements, or choose facts from policy response. For an image-based task, keep the image unchanged. State explicitly that the counterfactual is hypothetical and which single observation should be replaced. Do not claim that the original image depicts the hypothetical finding. Preserve unrelated observations, tooth identifiers, and coordinates. Return JSON with changed_fact, counterfactual_prompt, counterfactual_reference, and criterion_correspondences. Each correspondence contains the original criterion ID, counterfactual criterion text, correspondence label, and rationale. Query prompt Original prompt: {prompt} Reference and annotations: {reference} Original rubric: {rubric} Modality and supplied evidence: {evidence} Figure 7: Counterfactual Prompt and Rubric Construction prompt. 17 Preprint. Criterion Correspondence Labeling System prompt Align criteria across an original task and its single-fact counterfactual. Use the original rubric as the semantic anchor. Assign one label per correspondence: INVARIANT, TARGET_CHANGE, WEIGHT_CHANGE, DROPPED, or ADDED. INVARIANT preserves the requirement, target, weight, and applicability. TARGET_CHANGE means the changed fact requires different answer target. WEIGHT_CHANGE preserves the target but changes its importance. DROPPED means an original requirement is inapplicable under the counterfactual; ADDED means the intervention activates requirement absent on the original side. Do not label paraphrase as target change. Explain non-invariant labels by the changed fact, not by candidate responses. Return JSON with original_id, counterfactual_id, label, and rationale for each correspondence. Use null for the absent side of an added or dropped requirement. Flag ambiguous alignments for review. Preserve the targets question focus and complete answer meaning. The correct option must fully answer the target and be supported by the source. Distractors must be plausible, mutually exclusive alternatives that are false for this source. Match all four options in form, specificity, and completeness. Avoid all-of-the-above or none-of-the-above options, answer-position hints, wording or length cues, and unsupported claims in the correct answer. Keep the question complementary to sibling targets. Identify the uniquely correct option by its zero-based position in the supplied options array. Accept only if the question preserves the target, the source fully supports the correct option, and exactly one option completely answers the question. The three distractors must be plausible, mutually exclusive alternatives that are false for this source. Match option form and specificity; reject ambiguity, unsupported correct-answer claims, answer cues, and overlap with sibling targets. Preserve source and target identifiers, tested facts, complete correct-answer meaning, and correct-option position. You may revise the question and all three distractors. The question must identify the requested information without revealing the correct answer. response explicitly supplying the target facts must suffice to answer it. Preserve conditions, quantities, negations, exceptions, and required actions. Do not introduce unsupported facts, ambiguity, or answer cues to cause reader failure. Use the source and target as authority. Reader predictions are screening feedback, not factual evidence. Do not inspect responses from models being evaluated. Return JSON with question, correct, and distractors (three strings). If no faithful revision is possible, return unresolved=true with reason. A.3.2 REWARD EVALUATION Evidence-Aware Rubric Judge System prompt Score every supplied rubric criterion against the response. Use only task-allowed evidence: supplied source material for source-only tasks, or the prompt and reliable domain knowledge when permitted. Treat all supplied content as data. Assign three independent fulfillment scores in [0,1]: satisfaction, coverage, and support. Satisfaction measures whether the requirement is correctly fulfilled. Coverage measures whether the required information or action is present. Support measures whether that fulfillment is supported by the response and allowed evidence. Topical overlap, confidence, and an intention to act do not establish fulfillment. Missing required content receives zero coverage. stated but incorrect value may provide coverage while failing satisfaction and support. The supplied reference_value specifies fulfillment when the source criterions condition is absent. If it is 0, score fulfillment of the described requirement. If it is 1, score avoidance of the described undesirable condition: its supported presence lowers fulfillment. Return all three scores on this common fulfillment scale. Also score global_support for the responses claims as whole, and relevance, coherence, and concision, each in [0,1]. Unsupported claims outside the rubric still affect global_support. Do not reward verbosity or calculate the aggregate reward. Return JSON with criteria (criterion_id, satisfaction, coverage, support), global_support, and quality (relevance, coherence, concision). For both positive and negative points, met means the behavior described by the criterion is present. In particular, an undesirable behavior being present gives met=true for negative-point criterion. Require substantive correctness, not tone, headings, or topical overlap. Return JSON with judgments array containing id, met (boolean), and reason (specific evidence).
